examples.knowledge_point: Solving for an Unknown Given the Determinant
examples.problem: Given that the determinant of  $[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 2 \\ k & 4 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]$ is $2,$ find the value of the constant $k.$
examples.worked_solution:
Let's use our formula to find an expression for the determinant in terms of $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 2 \\ k & 4 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}| & =3|\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}k & 4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(12-10)-1(3k-0)+2(2k-0) \\  & =3\cdot 2-1\cdot 3k+2\cdot 2k \\  & =6-3k+4k \\  & =k+6\end{aligned}
$$

Since the determinant of the matrix is $2,$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}k+6 & =2 \\ k & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $Q$ given below?

- $det(Q)=-5$
- $det(Q)=1$
- $Q$ is **not** a singular matrix

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Q) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =1|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(9-5)-1(6-3)-1(10-9) \\  & =1\cdot 4-1\cdot 3-1\cdot 1 \\  & =4-3-1 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(Q)=0$, the matrix is singular. 

Therefore, none of the statements are true.

submitted_fields.submitted_value: None of the given statements are true
